Page: https://ratmath.com/numtheory/number-fields.html

Number fields

## Rings of integers

In Q(5​) the number (1+5​)/2 is a root of x2−x−1: it has a denominator, yet it behaves like a whole number. The algebraic integers of a number field form a ring, a lattice of rank n inside the field, and finding a basis of it is the first step of everything else: discriminants, prime ideals, class groups, units.

### A field and its integers

A number field is K=Q(α) for a root α of an irreducible polynomial; here it is a `NumberField` from `@ratmath/algebraic` (re-exported), or just the coefficients of the polynomial, constant first. An element of K is an algebraic integer when it is a root of a monic polynomial with whole coefficients. They form the ring OK​, and OK​ has a basis ω1​=1,ω2​,…,ωn​ over Z: an integral basis.

```js
import { NumberField, ringOfIntegers } from "@ratmath/numtheory";

const K = new NumberField([-8n, -2n, -1n, 1n]);   // α³ − α² − 2α − 8 = 0, Dedekind's field
const O = ringOfIntegers(K);
O.basis;            // 1, α, (1/2)α + (1/2)α²
O.discriminant;     // -503n
O.index;            // 2n: Z[α] has index 2 in the ring of integers
O.signature;        // [1, 1]: one real embedding, one pair of complex ones

O.contains(K.gen.mul(K.gen).add(K.gen).div(K.of(2n)));   // true: (α² + α)/2 is an integer
O.coordinates(K.gen.mul(K.gen));                         // 0, -1, 2: α² = −ω₂ + 2ω₃
String(O.element([0, 0, 1]));                            // "(1/2)α + (1/2)α²"
```

The quadratic case is the familiar one: Z[d​] when d≡2,3(mod4), and Z[(1+d​)/2] when d≡1(mod4).

```js
ringOfIntegers(NumberField.quadratic(5)).basis;     // 1, 1/2 + (1/2)√5
ringOfIntegers(NumberField.quadratic(-5)).basis;    // 1, √(-5)
ringOfIntegers([-19n, 0n, 0n, 1n]).basis;           // 1, α, 1/3 + (1/3)α + (1/3)α²   (α³ = 19)
```

### The discriminant

The discriminant of the field is dK​=det(Tr(ωi​ωj​)), the squared volume of the lattice OK​. It does not depend on the basis. For the lattice Z[α] the same determinant is the discriminant of the polynomial, and the two differ by the square of the index:

disc(f)=[OK​:Z[α]]2⋅dK​.
So only primes whose square divides disc(f) can divide the index. For Dedekind's field, disc(f)=−2012=−22⋅503, and the index is 2.

```js
O.polyDiscriminant;     // -2012n
O.traceMatrix;          // [[3, 1, 3], [1, 5, 18], [3, 18, 29]], with determinant −503
fieldDiscriminant([1n, 1n, 1n, 1n, 1n]);    // 125n: the fifth roots of unity
fieldDiscriminant([-2n, 0n, 0n, 0n, 1n]);   // -2048n: Q(⁴√2)
O.ramifiedPrimes;       // [503n]: the primes dividing the discriminant
```

### How the basis is found: Round 2

Start with the order O=Z[θ], where θ is α scaled to be integral, and enlarge it one prime at a time. For a prime p, let Ip​ be the radical of pO: the elements with some power in pO. The theorem of Pohst and Zassenhaus says that

O′={x∈K:xIp​⊆Ip​}
is an order containing O, and that O′=O exactly when O is already maximal at p. Both steps are linear algebra over Fp​. The radical is the kernel of x↦xpk on O/pO once pk≥n (or of the trace form when p>n), and O′ comes from the kernel of the map sending x to multiplication by x on Ip​/pIp​. Repeat until nothing grows, for each p with p2∣disc(f).

```js
O.steps;
// [{ p: 2n, exponent: 2, indexExponent: 1, rounds: 1, note: "the order grows by index 2 in 1 round" }]

ringOfIntegers([-19n, 0n, 0n, 1n]).steps.map((s) => s.note);
// ["the order grows by index 3 in 1 round", "already maximal at 19"]
```

The polynomial need not be monic or have whole coefficients: the generator is rescaled inside, and `O.scale` says by how much. The discriminant of the polynomial has to be factored, which is the one step that can be slow for large coefficients.

### Why Dedekind's field is famous

One might hope that OK​=Z[β] for a well-chosen β, as in quadratic fields. In Dedekind's field no β works. The prime 2 splits into three different prime ideals of norm 2 (see [Prime ideals](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/prime-ideals.html)); if OK​ were Z[β], those primes would correspond to three different linear factors of a cubic modulo 2, and there are only two linear polynomials modulo 2. So every Z[β] has even index.

Next: how primes factor in OK​, in [Prime ideals](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/prime-ideals.html); then [Class groups](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/class-groups.html) and [Units](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/units.html).

### Try it

```js
// pure cubic fields Q(∛m): the integral basis depends on m mod 9
for (const m of [2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 12, 17, 19, 26, 28]) {
  const O = ringOfIntegers([BigInt(-m), 0n, 0n, 1n]);
  PRINT(`m = ${m}`.padEnd(8), `disc ${O.discriminant}`.padEnd(12), `index ${O.index}`.padEnd(9), O.basis.join(",  "));
}
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/numtheory/prime-ideals.html

Number fields

## Prime ideals

In Z[−5​], 6=2⋅3=(1+−5​)(1−−5​), and none of the four factors can be broken further. Unique factorisation of numbers is lost. It comes back for ideals: every ideal is a product of prime ideals in exactly one way.

### How a prime decomposes

In the ring of integers O of a field of degree n, a rational prime p generates an ideal that factors as

pO=P1e1​​⋯Pgeg​​,i∑​ei​fi​=n,
where fi​ is the residue degree, O/Pi​≅Fpfi​​, and ei​ the ramification index. The prime is inert when pO is itself prime, ramified when some ei​>1 (exactly the primes dividing the discriminant), and splits completely when there are n primes of degree 1.

```js
import { NumberField, ringOfIntegers } from "@ratmath/numtheory";

const K = NumberField.quadratic(-5);
const O = ringOfIntegers(K);
O.describePrime(2).text;     // "2·O = (2, 1 + √(-5))²"                    ramified
O.describePrime(3).text;     // "3·O = (3, 1 + √(-5)) · (3, 2 + √(-5))"    splits
O.describePrime(11).text;    // "11·O = (11)"                              inert

const [P2] = O.primesAbove(2);
[P2.p, P2.e, P2.f, P2.norm];   // [2n, 2, 1, 2n]
P2.generators;                 // 2, 1 + √(-5): every prime ideal has two generators, one of them p
```

### Dedekind and Kummer

When p does not divide the index [O:Z[α]], the decomposition can be read from the polynomial: factor f modulo p,

f≡g1e1​​⋯grer​​(modp)⟹Pi​=(p, gi​(α)),fi​=deggi​.
For Q(−5​): x2+5≡(x+1)2(mod2), ≡(x+1)(x+2)(mod3), and it is irreducible modulo 11. That is the table above.

When p divides the index the recipe fails, and Dedekind's cubic x3−x2−2x−8 is the standard example: modulo 2 the polynomial is x2(x+1), which suggests a ramified prime, while in truth 2 splits completely.

```js
const D = ringOfIntegers(new NumberField([-8n, -2n, -1n, 1n]));
D.describePrime(2).text;
// "2·O = (2, (3/2)α + (1/2)α²) · (2, 1 + (1/2)α + (1/2)α²) · (2, 1 + α)"
D.primesAbove(2).map((P) => [P.e, P.f]);     // [[1, 1], [1, 1], [1, 1]]
D.describePrime(503).text;                   // "503·O = (503, 204 + α) · (503, 149 + α)²"
D.describePrime(5).text;                     // "5·O = (5, 4 + α) · (5, 3 + α²)": degrees 1 and 2
```

The library does not use the recipe as its method. For every prime it splits the finite ring A=O/pO directly: the radical of A is found as in Round 2; modulo the radical, A is a product of fields, one for each prime, and the elements fixed by x↦xp form a copy of Fpg​ whose idempotents cut the product apart. The ramification index of each prime is then the valuation of p. When the recipe applies, the second generator shown is the one it gives.

### Ideals

An ideal is kept as a basis over Z in Hermite normal form, so two ideals are equal exactly when their matrices are. Its norm is the index [O:I], and the norm of a principal ideal is the absolute value of the norm of its generator.

```js
const I = O.ideal(6);
String(I);              // "(2, 1 + √(-5))² · (3, 1 + √(-5)) · (3, 2 + √(-5))"
I.norm;                 // 36

const A = O.ideal(K.of([[1n, 1n], [1n, 1n]]));   // the ideal generated by 1 + √−5
String(A);              // "(2, 1 + √(-5)) · (3, 1 + √(-5))"
A.norm;                 // 6

const [P3, Q3] = O.primesAbove(3);
const J = P2.toIdeal().mul(P3);
J.equals(A);                         // true
J.basis;                             // 6, 1 + √(-5)
J.mul(J.inverse()).isOne;            // true: fractional ideals form a group
P3.toIdeal().add(Q3).isOne;          // true: different primes are coprime
P2.toIdeal().pow(2).equals(O.ideal(2));   // true
```

So the two factorisations of 6 are the same four prime ideals grouped in two ways: 2=P22​, 3=P3​Q3​, 1+−5​=P2​P3​, 1−−5​=P2​Q3​. The numbers 2, 3 and 1±−5​ are irreducible because P2​, P3​, Q3​ are not principal, which is the subject of [Class groups](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/class-groups.html).

### Valuations

The exponent of a prime P in an element or an ideal is its valuation vP​. It is computed with one multiplication per step: there is an element τ with τP⊆pO but τ∈/pO, and vP​(x) is the number of times x can be multiplied by τ/p and stay integral.

```js
P2.valuation(8);                              // 6: 8 = 2³ and 2 = P₂²
P2.valuation(K.of([[1n, 1n], [1n, 1n]]));     // 1
P2.valuation(K.of([[1n, 4n]]));               // -4: valuations of fractions are negative
P2.valuation(I);                              // 2
I.factor().map((f) => [String(f.prime), f.exponent]);
// [["(2, 1 + √(-5))", 2], ["(3, 1 + √(-5))", 1], ["(3, 2 + √(-5))", 1]]
```

Factoring an ideal needs only the factorisation of its norm into rational primes: the primes above those are the only candidates, and a valuation settles each.

### Try it

```js
// how the primes up to 60 behave in Q(∛2): the pattern follows p mod 3 and whether 2 is a cube mod p
const O = ringOfIntegers([-2n, 0n, 0n, 1n]);
for (const p of primes(60)) {
  const d = O.describePrime(p);
  PRINT(String(p).padStart(2), d.kind.padEnd(18), d.primes.map((P) => `e=${P.e} f=${P.f}`).join(",  "));
}
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/numtheory/class-groups.html

Number fields

## Class groups

The class group measures how far a ring of integers is from unique factorisation. Its elements are the ideals up to multiplication by a number; it is finite; it is trivial exactly when every ideal is principal. Here it is computed with a proof, not a heuristic.

### The group

Two ideals are in the same class when one is the other times a field element. Classes multiply, the principal ideals are the identity class, and the resulting group Cl(K) is finite. Its order is the class number h.

```js
import { NumberField, idealClassGroup, ringOfIntegers } from "@ratmath/numtheory";

const K = NumberField.quadratic(-5);
const cl = idealClassGroup(K);
cl.h;              // 2n
cl.structure;      // [2n]: a cyclic group of order 2
cl.generators;     // [(2, 1 + √(-5))], as an Ideal
cl.proven;         // true

const O = ringOfIntegers(K);
const [P2] = O.primesAbove(2);
const [P3] = O.primesAbove(3);
cl.classOf(P2);                    // [1n]: the non-trivial class
cl.isPrincipal(P2);                // { principal: false, generator: null }
cl.isPrincipal(P2.toIdeal().mul(P3));
// { principal: true, generator: 1 + √(-5) }
```

`structure` lists invariant factors d1​∣d2​∣⋯: the group is Z/d1​×Z/d2​×⋯, with one generator ideal for each. `classOf` gives the exponents of an ideal's class on those generators.

```js
const C = idealClassGroup([-65n, 0n, 0n, 1n]);     // Q(∛65)
String(C);          // "class group of Q(α), α a root of x³ − 65: C3 × C6, h = 18"
C.structure;        // [3n, 6n]

const [T] = C.order.primesAbove(2);
C.classOf(T);       // [1n, 5n]
C.orderOf(T);       // 6n
String(C.isPrincipal(T.toIdeal().pow(6)).generator);   // "49 + 24α − 9α²"
```

### Minkowski's bound

Geometry of numbers shows that every class contains an ideal of norm at most

MK​=nnn!​(π4​)r2​∣dK​∣​.
So the prime ideals of norm up to MK​ generate the class group, and there are finitely many. For Q(−5​) the bound is 2.8: the single prime above 2 generates everything, and it is not principal because a2+5b2=2 has no solution. That is the whole computation by hand.

```js
minkowskiBound(NumberField.quadratic(-5));       // 2n
minkowskiBound(NumberField.quadratic(-163));     // 8n: and 2, 3, 5, 7 are all inert, so h = 1
minkowskiBound([-65n, 0n, 0n, 1n]);              // 95n
C.factorBase.length;                             // 44 prime ideals above the primes up to 95
```

### Relations

Call the generating primes P1​,…,Pk​. An element x whose norm has only small prime factors gives a relation: (x)=∏Piai​​ means ∑ai​[Pi​]=0 in the class group. The relations form a lattice Λ⊆Zk, and

Cl(K)≅Zk/Λall​,
where Λall​ is the lattice of all relations. The library searches short vectors of O and of the primes themselves for elements with smooth norm, reduces the lattice they span, and reads off the Smith normal form. If the lattice found is Λ, its index h′ is a multiple of h: relations can be missing, never wrong.

### Certifying the answer

Systems such as PARI and Sage compute class groups quickly by assuming the generalised Riemann hypothesis, and offer a separate certification step. Here the certification is part of the answer, and no hypothesis is used.

The kernel of the relations gives units, with regulator R′ (see [Units](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/units.html)). Let G be the group generated by all relation elements and the roots of unity. Inside the group of all numbers supported on P1​,…,Pk​, the index of G is

hh′​⋅RR′​.
A prime ℓ divides this index exactly when some element of G is an ℓ-th power in K without being an ℓ-th power in G. That can be refuted: reduce G modulo a prime ideal q of degree 1 with ℓ∣q−1; raising to the power (q−1)/ℓ gives a homomorphism G/Gℓ→Z/ℓ, which kills every true ℓ-th power. Once as many independent such maps are found as the dimension of G/Gℓ, no hidden ℓ-th power exists.

- For each prime ℓ dividing h′, this test is run on G.

- Any other prime can only divide R′/R. Friedman proved that the regulator of every number field is at least 0.2052, so R′/R≤R′/0.2052, and for the primes ℓ up to that bound the same test is run on the units.

When every test passes, h′=h and R′=R. A test that fails says more than no: it names a product of the generators that every map takes for an ℓ-th power. The library takes the ℓ-th root of that product in the field (numerically at each embedding, then checked exactly), adds the root to the relation elements, and runs the computation again. The certificate counts these under `rootsTaken`.

```js
C.certificate;
// { method: "saturation", minkowskiBound: 95n, relations: 68, regulatorLowerBound: 0.2052,
//   unitIndexBound: 18, classNumberPrimes: [2, 3], primesChecked: 7, rootsTaken: 0 }

// the first relations found for Q(⁴√30) give 8; the test at 2 fails, and a square root brings it to 4
idealClassGroup([-30n, 0n, 0n, 0n, 1n], { certify: false }).h;    // 8n, marked proven: false
idealClassGroup([-30n, 0n, 0n, 0n, 1n]).h;                        // 4n, proven
```

Options: `certify: false` skips the proof (the result then has `proven: false`, and the true class number divides the one shown); `maxBound` (default 2000) refuses fields whose Minkowski bound is larger, since the number of primes grows with it; `maxIndexPrime` caps the primes ℓ tested. A cubic field with Minkowski bound near 100 takes about half a second; bound 1500 takes ten.

### Quadratic fields and forms

For a quadratic field the classes of ideals correspond to classes of [binary quadratic forms](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/quadratic-forms.html) of the same discriminant, and there the class number is found by listing reduced forms, with no search. Quadratic fields are certified that way: the relation computation has to agree with the count of forms. For a real quadratic field, forms give the narrow class number, which is twice the class number when the fundamental unit has norm +1.

```js
const R = idealClassGroup(NumberField.quadratic(79));
R.h;                                // 3n
R.certificate.narrowClassNumber;    // 6n: the fundamental unit 80 + 9√79 has norm +1

const F = NumberField.quadratic(-23);
const I = formToIdeal([2, 1, 3], F);   // the form 2x² + xy + 3y² as an ideal
String(I);                             // "(2, 3/2 + (1/2)√(-23))"
idealClassGroup(F).orderOf(I);         // 3n
```

For imaginary quadratic fields the class number is also a special value of an L-function, h=L(0,χD​) when D: see [Zeta and L values](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/l-values.html).

### Try it

```js
// class groups of the pure cubic fields Q(∛m), each one proven
for (const m of [2, 7, 11, 19, 20, 43, 63, 65, 113]) {
  const cl = idealClassGroup([BigInt(-m), 0n, 0n, 1n]);
  const s = cl.structure.length ? cl.structure.map((d) => `C${d}`).join(" × ") : "trivial";
  PRINT(`∛${m}`.padEnd(6), `h = ${cl.h}`.padEnd(8), s.padEnd(10), `bound ${cl.minkowskiBound}`.padEnd(10), `primes tested: ${cl.certificate.primesChecked}`, cl.certificate.rootsTaken ? `roots taken: ${cl.certificate.rootsTaken}` : "");
}
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/numtheory/units.html

Number fields

## Units

The units of a ring of integers are the elements of norm ±1. Dirichlet's theorem says what the group looks like: finitely many roots of unity, times a free group whose rank is fixed by the number of real and complex embeddings. Finding generators is harder than knowing they exist.

### Dirichlet's unit theorem

If K has r1​ real embeddings and r2​ pairs of complex ones, then

OK×​≅μw​×Zr,r=r1​+r2​−1,
where μw​ is the group of roots of unity in K. A set of r units generating the free part is a system of fundamental units.

```js
import { NumberField, unitGroup } from "@ratmath/numtheory";

const U = unitGroup(NumberField.quadratic(2));
U.rank;                 // 1
U.torsionOrder;         // 2: the roots of unity are ±1
U.fundamentalUnits;     // [1 + √2]
U.regulator;            // 0.881373587019543 = ln(1 + √2)

unitGroup(NumberField.gaussian()).torsionOrder;        // 4: ±1, ±i, and rank 0
unitGroup(NumberField.quadratic(-3)).torsionOrder;     // 6

const V = unitGroup([-2n, 0n, 0n, 1n]);                // Q(∛2): r₁ = 1, r₂ = 1, rank 1
String(V.fundamentalUnits[0]);                         // "1 + α + α²"

const W = unitGroup([2n, 0n, -4n, 0n, 1n]);            // totally real quartic: rank 3
W.fundamentalUnits.map(String);     // ["1 − α", "3 + 4α − α² − α³", "1 + 2α − α³"]
```

For a real quadratic field the fundamental unit comes from the [continued fraction](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/continued-fractions.html) of d​, and it can be large: for Q(94​) it is 2143295+22106494​.

### The regulator

Send a unit u to the vector of log∣σi​(u)∣ over the embeddings (doubled at complex ones). The image of the unit group is a lattice of rank r in the hyperplane where the coordinates sum to zero, and the regulator R is the determinant of any r×r minor of the matrix of fundamental units. A sub-system of units of index m has regulator mR, so a regulator certifies itself only together with a lower bound: this is how the units are proven fundamental, as described in [Class groups](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/class-groups.html).

```js
regulator([-2n, 0n, 0n, 1n]);          // 1.347377348329384
regulator([1n, -3n, 0n, 1n]);          // 0.8492874506461925: the cubic field inside Q(ζ₉)
V.certificate;
// { method: "saturation", …, regulatorLowerBound: 0.2052, unitIndexBound: 6, primesChecked: 3 }
```

For Q(32​): the unit found has regulator 1.347; if it were an m-th power of a smaller unit, that one would have regulator 1.347/m≥0.2052, so m≤6; and reductions modulo suitable primes show that it is not a square, a cube or a fifth power, up to sign. Hence it is fundamental.

### Roots of unity

If K has a real embedding the only roots of unity are ±1. Otherwise w divides N(q)−1 for every prime q not dividing w, which leaves few candidates after a handful of primes; each candidate m is settled by looking for a root of the cyclotomic polynomial Φm​ in K, exactly.

```js
const Z5 = unitGroup([1n, 1n, 1n, 1n, 1n]);     // Q(ζ₅)
Z5.torsionOrder;                // 10
String(Z5.rootOfUnity);         // "1 + α + α² + α³", which is −ζ₅⁴: a primitive tenth root
Z5.fundamentalUnits.map(String);   // ["α + α² + α³"], and its regulator is 2·ln((1 + √5)/2)
```

### Writing a unit on the fundamental ones

Every unit is ζt∏εiei​​ in one way. The exponents come from solving a linear system in the logarithms and rounding; the answer is then checked exactly.

```js
const K = new NumberField([-2n, 0n, 0n, 1n]);
const [eps] = V.fundamentalUnits;
V.exponents(eps.pow(7).neg());           // { torsion: 1, exponents: [7n] }: −ε⁷
V.exponents(K.of([[-1n, 1n], [1n, 1n]]));   // { torsion: 0, exponents: [-1n] }: α − 1 = 1/ε
V.isUnit(K.gen);                         // false: α has norm 2
```

Units are also what makes generators of principal ideals ambiguous: two generators differ by a unit. And they are the solutions of norm equations N(x)=±1, of which [Pell's equation](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/pell.html) is the quadratic case.

### Try it

```js
// real quadratic fields: the fundamental unit, its norm and the regulator
for (const d of [2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 13, 14, 19, 22, 31, 46, 61, 94]) {
  const U = unitGroup(NumberField.quadratic(d));
  const [e] = U.fundamentalUnits;
  PRINT(`√${d}`.padEnd(5), String(e).padEnd(28), `norm ${e.norm()}`.padEnd(9), `R = ${U.regulator.toFixed(6)}`);
}
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/numtheory/characters.html

L-functions

## Dirichlet characters

A Dirichlet character is a pattern of roots of unity that repeats modulo q and respects multiplication. Characters pick out residue classes the way sines and cosines pick out frequencies, which is how Dirichlet proved that every progression a,a+q,a+2q,… with gcd(a,q)=1 contains infinitely many primes.

### Definition and numbering

A character modulo q is a function χ on the integers with χ(mn)=χ(m)χ(n), χ(n+q)=χ(n), and χ(n)=0 exactly when gcd(n,q)>1. Its nonzero values are roots of unity. There are φ(q) characters modulo q, and under multiplication they form a group isomorphic to the units modulo q.

That isomorphism can be made explicit, and Conrey's numbering (the one used by the LMFDB) does so: for each m coprime to q there is a character χq​(m,⋅), with χq​(m,n)=χq​(n,m). For an odd prime power pe with least primitive root g,

χpe​(ga,gb)=exp(φ(pe)2πiab​),
with a similar rule for powers of 2 using ±5a, and a product over the prime powers of q.

```js
import { dirichletCharacter, dirichletGroup } from "@ratmath/numtheory";

const chi = dirichletCharacter(7, 3);
String(chi);            // "χ_7(3, ·)"
chi.order;              // 6
chi.exponent(2);        // 1/3: χ(2) = exp(2πi/3), exactly
chi.exponents();        // [null, 0, 1/3, 1/6, 2/3, 5/6, 1/2] for n = 0, …, 6
chi.value(2);           // { re: -0.5, im: 0.866… }
chi.parity;             // "odd": χ(−1) = −1
```

Values are kept exactly as fractions t with χ(n)=e2πit; `value` gives the complex number in doubles, and `at(n)` gives 0,1,−1 as BigInts for a real character.

### The group of characters

```js
const G = dirichletGroup(15);
G.order;                 // 8
G.structure;             // [2, 4]: the group is Z/2 × Z/4, like the units mod 15
G.characters.map((c) => [c.number, c.order, c.conductor, c.parity]);
// [1, 1, 1, even] [2, 4, 15, even] [4, 2, 5, even] [7, 4, 5, odd]
// [8, 4, 15, even] [11, 2, 3, odd] [13, 4, 5, odd] [14, 2, 15, odd]

String(dirichletCharacter(15, 2).mul(dirichletCharacter(15, 2)));    // "χ_15(4, ·)": numbers multiply
String(dirichletCharacter(3, 2).mul(dirichletCharacter(5, 2)));      // "χ_15(2, ·)": moduli combine
String(dirichletCharacter(15, 2).conjugate());                       // "χ_15(8, ·)"
```

The orthogonality relations are what make characters useful: summing over all characters isolates one residue class.

χmodq∑​χ(a)χ(b)​={φ(q)0​a≡b(modq), gcd(a,q)=1otherwise.​

```js
G.orthogonality(2, 2);     // { re: 8, im: 0 }
G.orthogonality(2, 7);     // { re: 0, im: 0 }
```

### Conductors and primitive characters

A character modulo 15 may really come from a smaller modulus: χ15​(11,⋅) only depends on n modulo 3, wherever it is not zero. The smallest such modulus is the conductor, and a character is primitive when its conductor is its modulus. Every character is induced by exactly one primitive character.

```js
const c = dirichletCharacter(15, 11);
c.conductor;               // 3
String(c.primitive());     // "χ_3(2, ·)"
G.primitive.map((x) => x.number);                 // [2, 8, 14]
String(dirichletCharacter(5, 2).induce(15));      // "χ_15(7, ·)"
```

For a primitive character the Gauss sum τ(χ)=∑a​χ(a)e2πia/q has absolute value exactly q​; it is the constant in the functional equation of the L-function.

### Real characters and the Kronecker symbol

The characters with values in {0,1,−1} are the quadratic ones. For a discriminant D, the [Kronecker symbol](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/reciprocity.html) n↦(nD​) is a character modulo ∣D∣, primitive exactly when D is a fundamental discriminant. It records how primes split in Q(D​): p splits when the symbol is 1, is inert when it is −1, and ramifies when it is 0.

```js
const k = kroneckerCharacter(-23);
String(k);                               // "χ_23(22, ·)"
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7].map((n) => k.at(n));   // [1n, 1n, 1n, 1n, -1n, 1n, -1n]
k.isPrimitive;                           // true
k.gaussSum();                            // { re: 0, im: 4.7958… }: i·√23
String(kroneckerCharacter(-4));          // "χ_4(3, ·)"
String(kroneckerCharacter(5));           // "χ_5(4, ·)"
```

What characters are for: the L-functions L(s,χ)=∑χ(n)n−s, in [Zeta and L values](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/l-values.html).

### Try it

```js
// the character table mod 12: rows are the characters χ_12(m, ·), columns the units n
const G = dirichletGroup(12);
const units = G.characters.map((c) => c.number);
PRINT("m \\ n".padEnd(8), units.map((n) => String(n).padStart(4)).join(""), "   order  conductor");
for (const c of G.characters) {
  PRINT(String(c.number).padEnd(8), units.map((n) => String(c.at(n)).padStart(4)).join(""), `   ${c.order}      ${c.conductor}`);
}
PRINT("");
PRINT("row sums:", G.characters.map((c) => units.reduce((s, n) => s + c.at(n), 0n)).join(" "), "  (only the principal character does not sum to zero)");
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/numtheory/l-values.html

L-functions

## Zeta and L values

ζ(2)=π2/6, ζ(−1)=−1/12, 1−31​+51​−⋯=π/4: special values of zeta and L functions carry arithmetic. Some are exact, and those are returned exactly. Everywhere else the value comes as an interval with rational endpoints that provably contains it.

### The functions

For a [Dirichlet character](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/characters.html) χ,

L(s,χ)=n≥1∑​nsχ(n)​=p∏​(1−psχ(p)​)−1(Res>1),
and the Riemann zeta function is the case of the trivial character. Each extends to the whole complex plane, with a single pole at s=1 when χ is principal and none otherwise.

### Exact values

At the non-positive integers the values are rational numbers given by Bernoulli numbers, ζ(−n)=−Bn+1​/(n+1), and at the positive even integers Euler's formula gives a rational multiple of a power of π.

```js
import { bernoulli, zetaExact, lValueExact, kroneckerCharacter, dirichletCharacter } from "@ratmath/numtheory";

[0, 1, 2, 4, 6, 12].map(bernoulli);    // 1, -1/2, 1/6, -1/30, 1/42, -691/2730
zetaExact(-1);                 // -1/12
zetaExact(-3);                 // 1/120
zetaExact(-2);                 // 0: a trivial zero
String(zetaExact(2));          // "π^2/6"
String(zetaExact(12));         // "691π^12/638512875"
zetaExact(12).coefficient;     // 691/638512875
```

For a character the same holds with generalised Bernoulli numbers: L(1−k,χ)=−Bk,χ​/k, where Bk,χ​=qk−1∑a=1q​χ(a)Bk​(a/q). For a real character the value is a Rational; for a complex one it lies in the cyclotomic field of the character's order.

```js
lValueExact(kroneckerCharacter(-23), 0);     // 3
lValueExact(kroneckerCharacter(-163), 0);    // 1
lValueExact(kroneckerCharacter(-4), 0);      // 1/2
lValueExact(kroneckerCharacter(5), -1);      // -2/5
String(lValueExact(dirichletCharacter(5, 2), 0));   // "3/5 + (1/5)ζ4": (3 + i)/5
```

The first lines are the class number formula. For a negative fundamental discriminant D, with w roots of unity in Q(D​),

h(D)=2w​L(0,χD​)=2πw∣D∣​​L(1,χD​).
So L(0,χ−23​)=3 is the class number of Q(−23​), found on the [Class groups](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/class-groups.html) page by entirely different means, and L(0,χ−163​)=1 is the reason eπ163​ is so nearly a whole number.

### Enclosures

At other points there is no closed form. `zetaValue` and `lValue` return a `RationalInterval` narrower than 2−bits (64 by default) that contains the true value. The argument is given exactly: a whole number, a fraction as text, or `[σ, t]` for the point σ+it of the plane, in which case the result is `{ re, im }`.

```js
import { zetaValue, lValue, hurwitzZeta } from "@ratmath/numtheory";

const z = zetaValue(3);                 // Apéry's constant
z.compactedDecimalInterval();           // "1.202056903159594285[38:41]"
zetaValue(3, { bits: 200 });            // sixty digits

zetaValue("1/2").low.toNumber();        // -1.4603545088095868

const w = zetaValue(["1/2", 14]);       // near the first zero, 1/2 + 14.1347…i
[w.re.low.toNumber(), w.im.low.toNumber()];     // [0.02224114…, -0.10325812…]

lValue(kroneckerCharacter(-4), 1).compactedDecimalInterval();    // "0.7853981633974483096[1:3]" = π/4
lValue(kroneckerCharacter(8), 1).low.toNumber();                 // 0.6232252401402305 = ln(1 + √2)/√2
lValue(dirichletCharacter(7, 3), [2, 5]);                        // { re, im }: a complex character, off the real line
```

The last real example is the class number formula for a real quadratic field: hlnε=2D​​L(1,χD​), here with h=1 and the unit ε=1+2​ from the [Units](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/units.html) page.

### How the enclosures are proved

Every L-function is a combination of Hurwitz zeta functions ζ(s,a)=∑n≥0​(n+a)−s:

L(s,χ)=q−sa=1∑q​χ(a)ζ(s,qa​).
And ζ(s,a) is computed by the Euler–Maclaurin formula: sum the first N terms directly, replace the rest by an integral, and correct with Bernoulli numbers,

ζ(s,a)=n=0∑N−1​(n+a)s1​+s−1(N+a)1−s​+2(N+a)s1​+j=1∑M​(2j)!B2j​​(N+a)s+2j−1s(s+1)⋯(s+2j−2)​+R,
with the remainder bounded explicitly:

∣R∣≤(2π)2M4∣s(s+1)⋯(s+2M−1)∣​⋅σ+2M−1(N+a)−(σ+2M−1)​,σ=Res>1−2M.
The formula holds wherever the bound makes sense, which is how it reaches the left half plane and the critical strip. Every operation is done in ball arithmetic: a midpoint and a radius, with each rounding added to the radius, and exponentials, logarithms, sines and cosines carrying their own error bounds. The remainder bound is added at the end. At s=1 the poles of the individual ζ(s,a/q) cancel because ∑χ(a)=0, and the limit is taken exactly.

```js
hurwitzZeta(2, "1/4").low.toNumber();   // 17.197329154507… = π² + 8G, with G Catalan's constant

// an enclosure contains the exact value where there is one
const e = zetaValue(-5, { bits: 100 });
const x = zetaExact(-5);                // -1/252
e.low.lessThanOrEqual(x) && x.lessThanOrEqual(e.high);    // true
```

Limits: the modulus of the character is at most 5000 for enclosures, and the cost grows with the modulus and with the height ∣t∣. For the zeros of ζ, with proof that they lie on the critical line, see the gamma and zeta page of [@ratmath/complex](https://ratmath.com/complex/gamma-zeta.html).

### Try it

```js
// the class number formula, three ways, for negative fundamental discriminants
for (const D of [-3, -4, -7, -8, -15, -20, -23, -47, -71, -163]) {
  const chi = kroneckerCharacter(D);
  const w = D === -3 ? 6 : D === -4 ? 4 : 2;
  const L1 = lValue(chi, 1, { bits: 40 });
  const fromL1 = (w * Math.sqrt(-D) * L1.low.toNumber()) / (2 * Math.PI);
  const exact = lValueExact(chi, 0).multiply(new Rational(BigInt(w), 2n));
  PRINT(`D = ${D}`.padEnd(10), `(w/2)·L(0, χ) = ${exact}`.padEnd(22), `from L(1, χ): ${fromL1.toFixed(9)}`.padEnd(30), `forms: ${classNumber(D)}`);
}
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/numtheory/padic.html

p-adic numbers

## p-adic numbers

Measure a number by how often p divides it, and the integers acquire a new completion: numbers with infinitely many digits to the left. Here a p-adic number is a rule that produces as many digits as you ask for, exactly.

### Valuation and the p-adic size

For a rational x=0, vp​(x) is the exponent of p in x and ∣x∣p​=p−vp​(x). So ∣50/27∣5​=1/25 and ∣50/27∣3​=27: being divisible by p makes a number small. This size satisfies the strong triangle inequality ∣x+y∣p​≤max(∣x∣p​,∣y∣p​), and with the ordinary size it gives the product formula ∣x∣∏p​∣x∣p​=1.

```js
import { padic, padicValuation, padicNorm, expansion, henselRoot, teichmuller } from "@ratmath/numtheory";

padicValuation("50/27", 5n);          // 2
String(padicNorm("50/27", 3n));       // "27"
padic("50/27", 3n).toString();        // "…00000000000000001.212"
```

### Infinitely many digits to the left

Completing Q with ∣⋅∣p​ gives Qp​, whose elements are ∑i≥v​di​pi with digits 0≤di​<p, written right to left. In Z5​, …4444=−1: add 1 and every digit carries. A rational's expansion is eventually periodic, and conversely.

```js
padic(-1, 5n).toString();      // "…44444444444444444444"
padic("1/3", 5n).toString();   // "…31313131313131313132": 3 times it is …0001
expansion("1/3", 5n);          // { valuation: 0, preperiod: [2n], period: [3n, 1n] }
padic("1/10", 5n).toString();  // "…2222222222222222222.3"
```

### Lazy and exact

A `Padic` is a rule: given N, it returns a rational r with vp​(x−r)≥N. Rationals are exact. A sum asks its parts for precision N; a product asks each for N minus the other's valuation; a quotient first finds the divisor's valuation. Nothing is fixed in advance, so asking for more digits reruns the whole computation to that depth, and results are cached. What cannot be decided by digits is reported: the valuation of a number that may be zero is searched for, and the search gives up with the code `"unknown-valuation"` rather than claiming a zero.

### Square roots and Hensel

For odd p, a unit u is a square in Zp​ exactly when it is a square mod p; for p=2, when u≡1(mod8). Then Newton's iteration from a root mod p converges p-adically, doubling the correct digits each step. `henselRoot` does the same for any polynomial, given a start r0​ with v(f(r0​))>2v(f′(r0​)).

```js
const i = padic(-1, 5n).sqrt();
i.toString();                   // "…40423140223032431212": a square root of −1 in Z₅
i.mul(i).toString();            // "…44444444444444444444"
padic(-7, 2n).sqrt();           // exists: −7 ≡ 1 (mod 8)
padic(2, 5n).sqrt();            // throws "not-a-square": 2 is not a square mod 5
henselRoot([-2, 0, 0, 1], 3, 5n).toString();   // "…21134404003204132203", the cube root of 2 ≡ 3 (mod 5)
```

### exp, log and roots of unity

The series expx=∑xn/n! converges when vp​(x)≥1 (≥2 for p=2), since vp​(n!)≤(n−1)/(p−1). The series log(1+y)=y−y2/2+… converges for vp​(y)≥1, and extends to every unit by logu=log(up−1)/(p−1); on the domain of exp the two are inverse. The Teichmüller representative ω(a)=limapn is the (p−1)-th root of unity congruent to a: in Z5​, ω(2) is the square root of −1 above.

```js
padic(5, 5n).exp().log().toString();    // "…000000000000000000010": back to 5
teichmuller(2n, 5n).toString();         // "…40423140223032431212"
teichmuller(2n, 5n).pow(4).toString();  // "…00000000000000000001"
```

### Try it

```js
// the expansions of a few rationals in Z_7, with their periods
for (const q of ["1/2", "-1/3", "5/6", "1/49", "22/7"]) PRINT(q, padic(q, 7n).toString(16), expansion(q, 7n));
// √2 in Z_7: ask for more digits and the computation reruns to that depth
const r = padic(2, 7n).sqrt();
PRINT(r.toString(10), "\n", r.toString(30));
PRINT("r² − 2 ≡ 0 mod 7^30:", r.mul(r).sub(2).mod(30) === 0n);
// but r² − 2 is exactly zero, and digits alone can never show that: the answer says so
try { r.mul(r).sub(2).valuation(); } catch (e) { PRINT(e.code); }
// log is a homomorphism: log(ab) = log a + log b
const a = padic(8, 7n), b = padic(15, 7n);
PRINT(a.mul(b).log().equalsTo(a.log().add(b.log()), 40));
// the product formula for 360/7
[2n, 3n, 5n, 7n].map((p) => [p, String(padicNorm("360/7", p))])
```
